content: Insect sting allergy refers to the allergic reaction that occurs in response to the bite or sting of an insect. The insects that typically cause allergic reactions can be categorized into two groups: stinging insects, such as wasps, bees, hornets, and ants, and biting insects, such as mosquitoes and ticks. Stinging insects inject venom into their victims, while biting insects usually introduce anti-coagulants into the skin. In most cases, individuals with insect sting allergies experience a localized allergic reaction at the site of the sting. This reaction is characterized by swelling, which is caused by the release of histamine and other chemicals from the tissues near the sting site. Such localized swelling can often be managed with the application of an anti-histamine ointment and the use of an ice pack. This type of reaction is common for all biting insects, and many people experience it to varying degrees. In some cases, mosquito bites can lead to a condition known as Skeeter Syndrome, which is a collection of symptoms that occur after a bite. This syndrome may be mistaken for a bacterial skin infection, such as cellulitis. However, in individuals who are anaphylactic, the allergic response can be much more severe. These individuals may experience a systemic reaction, where the allergic response spreads beyond the sting site and affects the entire body. This type of reaction is serious and can lead to anaphylaxis, a life-threatening condition. For individuals who experience systemic allergic reactions to insect stings, venom immunotherapy is a well-established treatment option in North America and Europe. This therapy significantly reduces the severity of allergic responses in such patients. The majority of people who are stung by insects experience only localized reactions. However, it is estimated that 5-10% of individuals will develop a generalized systemic reaction, which can range from symptoms like hives to more severe manifestations such as wheezing or even anaphylaxis. In the United States, approximately 40 deaths occur each year due to anaphylaxis caused by stinging insect allergies. Life-threatening reactions are observed in about 3% of adults and 0.4-0.8% of children.
